title: Software Architecture Styles
tagline: Compare layered, hexagonal, DDD bounded contexts, event-driven, and monolith vs microservices — and know which style fits which problem.

sections.content:
**Software architecture** is the set of significant decisions that shape a system's structure, coupling, and evolution. Choosing the wrong architecture does not crash a system on day one — it makes *changing* the system increasingly expensive over time. Choosing the right architecture keeps the system flexible precisely in the dimensions it needs to flex.

No single architecture is universally best. A side-project todo app and a global e-commerce platform have radically different constraints. The art is matching the **architectural style** — the high-level pattern of how components are organised and communicate — to the project's actual change rate, team size, scalability needs, and domain complexity. This lesson surveys five major styles: **layered** (the default), **hexagonal/ports-and-adapters** (testability-first), **Domain-Driven Design with bounded contexts** (complex domains), **event-driven** (decoupled async), and the **monolith vs microservices** spectrum.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    LAYERED["Layered\nPresentation → Business → Data"]
    HEX["Hexagonal\nDomain at centre, ports and adapters"]
    DDD["DDD Bounded Contexts\nSubdomains with explicit boundaries"]
    EVT["Event-Driven\nProducers, event bus, consumers"]
    MONO["Monolith\nSingle deployable unit"]
    MICRO["Microservices\nIndependent deployable services"]
    LAYERED -->|"evolves into"| HEX
    HEX -->|"applied to subdomains"| DDD
    DDD -->|"communication via"| EVT
    MONO -->|"decomposed into"| MICRO
sections.caption: Architecture styles are not mutually exclusive — a system may use hexagonal layout within each bounded context while services communicate through events.

sections.title: City Planning vs. Open Fields
sections.content:
A well-zoned city has residential areas (UI), commercial districts (business logic), and industrial zones (databases/infrastructure). Residents do not need to know how sewage works; they use taps and drains (abstractions). This is **layered architecture** — strict zones with defined interfaces between them.

**Hexagonal architecture** flips the metaphor: the city hall (domain) is at the centre, and every external service — the power grid (database), the road network (HTTP), the postal service (message queue) — plugs in via standardised connectors (ports). The city hall operates identically regardless of which power company supplies electricity.

**Microservices** are like independent city-states, each with its own government, budget, and infrastructure. Coordination requires diplomacy (APIs, contracts). The overhead is real — but each city-state can evolve independently and scale according to its own population. A small town does not need city-state independence; the overhead would crush it. Choose the model to match your actual scale.

**Layered Architecture** organises code into horizontal layers — Presentation (HTTP controllers, CLI), Business Logic (services, use cases), and Data (repositories, ORM). Each layer depends only on the layer below it. It is the default pattern for most web frameworks (MVC). Simple to understand, but the domain layer often ends up coupled to the database schema over time.

**Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters)** places the *domain* at the centre and defines *ports* — interfaces the domain expects (e.g. `UserRepository`, `EmailSender`). *Adapters* implement those ports for specific technologies (PostgreSQL adapter, SendGrid adapter). The domain has zero imports from framework or infrastructure code. Tests can run the entire domain with in-memory adapters — no database needed. This style was coined by Alistair Cockburn and maps directly to the Dependency Inversion Principle.

**Domain-Driven Design (DDD) with Bounded Contexts** addresses *organisational* complexity. Large systems have multiple distinct sub-domains (e.g. Billing, Inventory, Shipping), each with its own language (ubiquitous language), models, and rules. A *Bounded Context* is an explicit boundary within which a model is consistent. A `Product` in Billing (has a price and invoice line) is a different concept from `Product` in Inventory (has a warehouse location and SKU). DDD says: do not force one model to serve all contexts — let each context own its model.

**Event-Driven Architecture** decouples producers from consumers via an event bus or message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS). A service publishes `OrderPlaced`; the Inventory service, Email service, and Analytics service each consume it independently. No direct coupling between producer and consumers. Highly scalable and flexible for async workflows, but introduces complexity: message ordering, at-least-once delivery, and eventual consistency must be managed.

**Monolith vs Microservices:** A monolith is a single deployable unit — one process, one database, one codebase. It is the correct starting point for most projects: simple to develop, test, deploy, and debug. Microservices split the system into small, independently deployable services, each owning its data. This enables independent scaling, technology diversity, and team autonomy — but adds network latency, distributed transactions, service discovery, and operational complexity. The rule of thumb: start as a monolith, extract services when you have a proven scaling or team-autonomy bottleneck.

    DOMAIN["Domain\nOrderService impl"]

sections.caption: Hexagonal architecture: the domain is fully insulated. Swapping PostgreSQL for MongoDB or HTTP for gRPC requires changing only the relevant adapter, never the domain.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The hexagonal example shows the domain (createOrderService) accepting ports as arguments — in tests you pass in-memory fakes; in production you pass real adapters. The domain code is identical in both cases. The event bus example shows how publishing one `OrderPlaced` event drives three independent consumers with zero coupling between them.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: Bounded contexts make explicit that the same real-world entity (a Product) has intentionally different models in different business subdomains. An anti-corruption layer translates between contexts without polluting either model. The layered example shows strict unidirectional dependencies: no HTTP in the service, no database in the controller.

sections.content: **Start with a modular monolith, not microservices.** A monolith with clearly-defined internal module boundaries (e.g. `src/billing/`, `src/inventory/`) gives you 80% of microservices' organisational benefits with 5% of the operational overhead. When a module genuinely needs independent deployment or scaling, extract it into a service at that point — you will know *exactly* where the boundary is because you drew it months ago.

items: **Layered** separates Presentation, Business Logic, and Data into layers with unidirectional dependencies — the simplest starting point for most applications.
**Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters)** insulates the domain from all infrastructure code via interfaces, making the domain fully testable without databases or HTTP servers.
**DDD Bounded Contexts** model large systems as distinct subdomains, each with its own ubiquitous language and data model, connected via explicit anti-corruption layers.
**Event-Driven** decouples producers from consumers via an event bus, enabling async workflows and independent scaling at the cost of eventual consistency complexity.

**Start as a modular monolith** — extract microservices only when you have a proven, specific need (independent scaling, team autonomy). Premature decomposition multiplies operational complexity without benefit.

quiz.question: In layered architecture, in which direction should dependencies point?
options: Data layer imports from Business layer; Business layer imports from Presentation
Each layer can freely import from any other layer
Presentation imports from Business; Business imports from Data — but never the reverse
All layers import from a shared global configuration module
quiz.explanation: Layered architecture enforces strict unidirectional dependencies: Presentation → Business → Data. A controller may call a service; a service may call a repository; but a repository must never import from a service or controller.

quiz.question: What is a 'port' in hexagonal architecture?
options: A network TCP port number used by the service
An interface or abstract boundary defining what the domain needs from or exposes to the outside world
A database connection pool configuration
A Docker container port mapping
quiz.explanation: A port in hexagonal architecture is an interface (or abstract contract) — e.g. `OrderRepository` or `EmailSender`. Adapters implement these interfaces for specific technologies. The domain only knows the port, never the concrete adapter.

quiz.question: Why does DDD use separate models for the same real-world entity (e.g. 'Product') in different bounded contexts?
options: To avoid foreign key constraints between databases
Because different subdomains have different relevant attributes and rules — forcing one shared model creates unwanted coupling
To satisfy microservices requirements for independent deployment
Because shared models cause circular import errors in JavaScript
quiz.explanation: A 'Product' in Billing needs price and tax category; in Inventory it needs SKU and warehouse location. Forcing one model to serve both contexts causes both to be polluted with irrelevant fields and tightly coupled to each other's changes.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of event-driven architecture's decoupling?
options: Events are processed faster than direct HTTP calls
The producer does not need to know which consumers exist — new consumers can be added without changing the producer
Events are automatically stored and replayed on failure
Event-driven systems never experience data inconsistency
quiz.explanation: The key decoupling benefit: the `OrderPlaced` event producer (OrderService) does not know or care whether one, three, or ten services consume it. Adding the Analytics consumer required zero changes to OrderService. This is the Open/Closed Principle at the architectural level.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the recommended approach to monolith vs microservices for a new project?
options: Always start with microservices to avoid painful extraction later
Start with a modular monolith and extract services when specific scaling or autonomy needs are proven
Microservices are always better because they are independently deployable
Monoliths cannot support multiple developers working simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Premature microservices decomposition multiplies network complexity, distributed transaction difficulty, and operational overhead without benefit. A modular monolith delivers team organisation benefits early; extraction happens when actual bottlenecks appear.

quiz.question: What is an Anti-Corruption Layer in DDD?
options: A security layer that validates all API inputs
A translation component that converts models between bounded contexts without polluting either context's model
A database trigger that prevents invalid data from being inserted
A logging layer that tracks all cross-service communication
quiz.explanation: An Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) sits between two bounded contexts and translates models between them. It prevents the concepts and language of one context from leaking into another, keeping each context's model clean and coherent.

quiz.question: In hexagonal architecture, what is the key advantage of the domain having no imports from framework or database code?
options: The domain runs faster because it has no external dependencies
The entire domain can be tested with in-memory adapters — no database or HTTP server required
It satisfies JavaScript's circular dependency restrictions
It makes the domain code shorter and easier to read
quiz.explanation: With in-memory adapters implementing the domain's ports, you can run comprehensive domain tests without any I/O — no DB connections, no HTTP servers. Tests are fast, deterministic, and portable across environments.

quiz.question: Which architecture style is most appropriate for a system with many independent async workflows, such as sending emails, updating inventory, and logging analytics — all triggered by the same event?
options: Layered architecture
Monolith with shared database
Event-driven architecture
Hexagonal architecture
quiz.explanation: Event-driven architecture is ideal when one business event should trigger multiple independent downstream actions. Each consumer handles its concern independently; adding or removing a consumer requires no changes to the producer or other consumers.

quiz.question: What is 'ubiquitous language' in Domain-Driven Design?
options: Code written in a language that runs everywhere, such as JavaScript
A shared vocabulary used consistently by both developers and domain experts within a bounded context
An international naming convention for API endpoints
A design pattern for translating between different programming languages
quiz.explanation: Ubiquitous language is a common vocabulary agreed upon by developers and domain experts (e.g. business analysts) within a bounded context. Code class names, method names, and database columns use this same vocabulary — eliminating translation between 'business speak' and 'tech speak'.

quiz.question: What is a key operational disadvantage of microservices compared to a monolith?
options: Microservices cannot be deployed independently
Microservices require all teams to use the same programming language
Microservices introduce network latency, distributed transactions, and significant operational complexity
Microservices cannot scale horizontally
quiz.explanation: With microservices, what was a local function call becomes a network call — adding latency, failure modes, and the need for retries/circuit breakers. Transactions that span services require distributed coordination (sagas, eventual consistency). Service discovery, health checks, and container orchestration add substantial ops overhead.
